newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Croats accused of "ethnic engineering".
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Croats accused of "ethnic engineering".

text.p: Bosnian Croat authorities are systematically blocking the return of non-Croat refugees in towns adjacent to Croatia in clear violation of a 1995 peace agreement, an international watchdog agency reported on Monday.

Croat authorities orchestrated the torching of 25 homes in the town of Drvar last month as part of a campaign to discourage Serbs from moving back to the area, said the International Crisis Group (ICG), a private agency monitoring Bosnia's peace treaty.
"The vandalism in Drvar is sadly not an isolated event but part of a sustained campaign to prevent the return of minorities," the ICG report said.

Croat, Serb and Moslem authorities alike have contrived to block the return of war refugees not belonging to the majority group in areas they control, but Western monitors say almost all the abuses occur on Serb- and Croat-held territory.
Before the war, Drvar had a predominantly Serb population which fled after Croat forces captured the area at the close of Bosnia's conflict in 1995.
Drvar authorities have since encouraged Croats from towns in Serb or Moslem-held areas to move to the municipality, including some 2,000 soldiers serving in the Bosnian Croat militia.
"In effect, wartime ethnic cleansing has been replaced in peace by the more subtle 'ethnic engineering'," the report said.
The report blamed local officials from the ruling Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ), the police and Croat militia for organising the campaign of intimidation against Serb refugees.
ICG cited Drago Tokmakcija, head of the HDZ in Drvar and deputy mayor, Mayor Boro Malbasic and police officers Zvonko Banovic, Miroslav Frankic and Zarko Sokcic as "the most responsible" for abuses.
Franjo Tudjman, president of neighbouring Croatia and head of the HDZ, has long been accused of seeking to carve out "ethnically pure" territory along the border through his political proteges.
Croat authorities have denied any link to torching houses and say displaced Croats are being prevented from returning to their homes in Serb or Moslem-controlled areas.
The ICG called on major powers to exert maximum pressure on the nationalist Croatian government to ensure Bosnian Croats comply with the peace accords.

It said that when property of an ethnic minority is vandalised, the NATO-led peace force should remove and destroy an equal number of tanks or heavy artillery pieces from cantonment sites of the army in control of the area.
The "tank-for-a-house" response would be "measured and proportionate, easy to explain and transparently fair", the report said.
An election commission from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) recently investigated the house burnings in Drvar.
The commission, led by an international judge, removed a HDZ candidate from the municipal ballot in Drvar and threatened similar penalties in the future.
Croat authorities were also obstructing attempts by Moslems to return to their homes in the southern town of Stolac, U.N. human rights workers reported.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said two houses formerly inhabited by Moslems were set ablaze in Stolac last Friday shortly after reconstruction work had begun on a resettlement project for displaced Moslems.
A UNHCR spokeswoman called the incident "extremely worrying".
